tagline: Granite tunnels and climbing bridges shape a road built for slow sightseeing
intro: The Peter Norbeck Scenic Byway threads the Black Hills through rock tunnels, across spiraling bridges and among granite pinnacles and pine-covered mountains. The Federal Highway Administration lists this National Scenic Byway as 68 miles and allows four hours to drive it. The Forest Service highlights Mount Rushmore, Custer State Park, Needles Highway and Iron Mountain Road along the route. On the Needles Highway, that landscape includes ponderosa pine and Black Hills spruce forests, with birch and aspen surrounding the meadows.

Peter Norbeck planned the Needles Highway by marking its course on foot and horseback; construction finished in 1922. He then chose the layout of Iron Mountain Road in the 1930s and pressed ahead despite being told it could not be built. Its three tunnels frame Mount Rushmore, while pigtail bridges let the road gain or lose height quickly. The scenic byway was established in his honor on September 23, 1996.

For a circuit from Custer, take U.S. 16A east through Custer State Park, then follow Iron Mountain Road toward Keystone. South Dakota 244 leads west past Mount Rushmore; connect to SD 87 for the return toward Sylvan Lake. Continue south on the Needles Highway through the granite formations, then rejoin U.S. 16A toward Custer.

moments.title: Iron Mountain Road
moments.text: The pigtail bridges on Iron Mountain Road let vehicles climb or descend quickly, while three tunnels frame Mount Rushmore in the distance. The road was laid out specifically for slow sightseeing. Norbeck chose its course in the 1930s, persisting after being told the scheme was impossible. U.S. 16A was deliberately taken over Iron Mountain’s summit to provide views of Mount Rushmore. The park manager allows at least an hour for the 17-mile road, a measure of the pace this engineering calls for. A small memorial to Norbeck stands on the summit, beside the route he helped bring into being.
moments.notice: Three tunnels frame Mount Rushmore in the distance.

moments.title: Sylvan Lake
moments.text: Sylvan Lake owes its existence to a dam: Theodore Reder blocked Sunday Gulch Creek in 1891 to create it. The lake is in Custer State Park and serves as a starting point for excursions to Black Elk Peak and the Needles. The state park’s driving guide places Sylvan Lake along the Needles Highway, sharing that drive with the eroded opening of the Needle’s Eye. Its screen geography is different. In the 2007 film National Treasure: Book of Secrets, Sylvan Lake appears directly behind Mount Rushmore. The actual lake lies five miles southwest of the monument.

moments.title: Needles Eye Tunnel
moments.text: The Needle’s Eye has an opening made by wind, rain, freezing and thawing; the neighboring road tunnel was blasted through granite. Both belong to the Needles Highway, named for the slender granite formations along its course. Norbeck marked the road’s entire route on foot and horseback, and construction was completed in 1922. The drive passes ponderosa pine and Black Hills spruce forests, birch and aspen meadows, and rugged granite mountains. The park manager allows at least an hour for this 14-mile highway. Iron Creek Tunnel is the other granite passage on the drive.
moments.notice: The Needle’s Eye rock formation has an eroded opening beside the tunnel.

practical: Iron Mountain Road: Iron Mountain Road closes periodically in winter, depending on conditions and how quickly it can be cleared safely. (checked 2026-10-11)

Needles Eye Tunnel: Needles Eye Tunnel is 8 feet wide and 9 feet 9 inches high. Needles Highway closes to vehicles with the first snow and reopens April 1 or later, depending on conditions. (checked 2026-10-11)
